content: Retained placenta occurs in 0.5% to 3% of women after childbirth and is a significant cause of maternal mortality due to postpartum hemorrhage. Traditionally, retained placenta has been managed through manual removal or curettage under anesthesia. However, these procedures carry risks such as hemorrhage, infection, and uterine perforation. Medical management using prostaglandins has been proposed as a potentially safer alternative to avoid surgical intervention. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of prostaglandins in managing retained placenta. Researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries up to December 1, 2013, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, LILACS, SciELO, Web of Science, openSIGLE, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials. They also contacted study authors and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials comparing prostaglandins (or their analogues) with placebo, expectant management, tocolytic drugs, other prostaglandins, or surgical interventions for retained placenta following vaginal delivery of live singleton infants at 20 or more weeks of gestation. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated their quality, and extracted data. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Additional information was sought from the authors of the included studies. Three trials involving 244 women were included in the analysis. The studies were deemed to have a high risk of bias. The prostaglandins used were sulprostone (a prostaglandin E2 analogue) in 50 participants and misoprostol (a prostaglandin E1 analogue) in 194 participants, administered at doses of 250 mcg and 800 mcg, respectively. When compared to placebo, prostaglandins did not significantly reduce the rate of manual removal of the placenta (average risk ratio [RR] 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54 to 1.27), severe postpartum hemorrhage (RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.55 to 1.15), the need for blood transfusion (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.43 to 1.22), mean blood loss (mean difference [MD] -205.26 mL; 95% CI -536.31 to 125.79), or the mean time from injection to placental removal (MD -7.00 minutes; 95% CI -21.20 to 7.20). Side effects such as vomiting, headache, pain, and nausea were similar between the prostaglandin and placebo groups. However, shivering was significantly more common in women who received prostaglandins (RR 10.00; 95% CI 1.40 to 71.49). No data were available for the primary outcomes of maternal mortality or the need for additional therapeutic uterotonics. The authors concluded that the current evidence on the use of prostaglandins for managing retained placenta is limited and of very low quality. While prostaglandins appeared to reduce the need for manual removal of the placenta, severe postpartum hemorrhage, and blood transfusion, these differences were not statistically significant. Larger, well-designed studies are necessary to confirm whether these observed benefits are genuine or due to chance. Similarly, no significant differences were found between prostaglandins and placebo in terms of mean blood loss, time to placental removal, or most side effects, except for shivering, which was more frequent in the prostaglandin group. Given the poor quality of the included studies and the uncertainty of the effect estimates, the true impact of prostaglandins is likely to differ substantially. As a result, no recommendations can currently be made for changes to clinical practice. High-quality research in this area is urgently needed.
